pages.title: Tuval — the sticky note is the ticket
pages.description: A self-hostable workspace where an infinite canvas, your pages and your issue tracker are three views of one record. Promote a sticky note on this page and watch it turn up in the table and the sprint. AGPL-3.0 licensed, free for three people.
pages.claim: The sticky note is the ticket.
pages.lede: Not a copy of it. Not a link to it. One record, drawn on a canvas, listed in a table, worked in a sprint. The three panels below are live and they are all reading the same document.

bands.heading: One board, read three ways
bands.body: The left panel is the product's own renderer drawing a real document. The two beside it read that same document, and nothing is copied between them because there was only ever one of it. Switch the right panel to brief.md and the board comes out as markdown a coding agent can act on: every other whiteboard exports a picture, and a picture is the one thing a model cannot act on.

bands.heading: Tuesday's sticky is Friday's ticket
bands.body: Select a note, press one button, and it is an issue with a key on it. The card stands where the note stood and the arrow you drew stays attached, because where you put it was part of the thought. Rename it in the table and the canvas changes under your hand. Nothing is retyped, because nothing was ever copied.

bands.heading: Canvas
bands.body: A surface with no edges and no lag.
lines: Frames, connectors, sticky notes, pen, shapes, tables and mind maps
Images, PDFs placed page by page, live embeds and code blocks
Presentation mode, comments and version history
Templates, and importers for an existing Miro board or a Notion export

bands.heading: Pages and databases
bands.body: Where the same records get written down.
lines: A block editor with nested pages, mentions, backlinks and an inbox
Databases with twenty column types, formulas, rollups and relations
Table, board, list, gallery, calendar and timeline views over them
Publish a page to the web, or keep it behind the login

bands.heading: Issues
bands.body: The work, with keys on it.
lines: Issues with keys, cycles, projects, estimates and labels
Sub-issues, blocking relations, a board view and a burn-down
Promote a note or a paragraph into an issue where it stands
A card on a canvas points at the row it came from and refreshes from it

bands.heading: Getting your work in
bands.body: Switching is the expensive part, so here is exactly how far the importers go and where they stop.

points.title: A Miro board
points.body: A script pulls the board through Miro's own API and the mapper lays it out here: frames, sticky notes, shapes, text, connectors and images. Your token stays in your shell and never reaches this site.

points.title: A Notion export
points.body: Take the markdown export Notion gives you and the pages come in as pages, with their headings, lists, code blocks, tables and nesting intact. Databases arrive as databases, not as screenshots of them.

points.title: A tracker backlog
points.body: This one is not solved. There is no importer for Linear or Jira, so a backlog would be retyped. It is the hardest thing about switching and pretending otherwise would waste your afternoon.

bands.heading: One tool. One line on the invoice.
bands.body: Priced for a team that was paying three separate bills for the same afternoon's work. The code is AGPL either way; what is charged for is somebody else keeping the disks spinning.

points.title: Free
points.body: Up to three people, one gigabyte of files, and every board, page, database and issue there is. No card, no trial clock.

points.title: Team
points.body: {price} per {per} per {period}, VAT included, about {about}. Ten gigabytes each, up to two hundred people, and the API and webhooks so n8n and the rest can reach it.

points.title: Your own server
points.body: Nothing, for good. A Postgres and a bucket, your disks and your backups. No seat count, no phone-home, no feature held back to make the paid one look better.

bands.heading: Where it stops
bands.body: Written by one person, in Turkey. So here is the list a sales page leaves out, which is better read now than after you have moved a team across.

points.title: Live editing is unproven
points.body: The synchronisation is written and the channel is private, checked by the same policies as the board itself. It has never once been run with two people in the room.

points.title: No phone layout, deliberately
points.body: An infinite canvas on a six-inch screen is a worse product, not a smaller one. The effort goes into the desk instead.

points.title: No enterprise identity
points.body: Email, GitHub, Google and Apple sign-in, with roles enforced in the database. No SAML, no SCIM, no signed support agreement. If procurement needs those, this does not get approved.

points.title: Embeds sit on top
points.body: A live embed is a real iframe over the canvas, so an item stacked above one still draws behind it. A still preview will fix it.

bands.heading: Draw it once. Ship it from the same place.
bands.body: Start a board in the browser, or clone the repository and run the whole thing on a machine you own. Both are the same software.

pages.title: Infinite canvas and workspace | Tuval
pages.description: An infinite canvas with frames, connectors, sticky notes, tables and mind maps. Drawn on one canvas element, works offline, and every idea on it can become a tracked issue.
pages.claim: A surface with no edges and no lag.
pages.lede: One canvas element, a dirty-flag render loop, and a document that lives in your browser before it lives anywhere else. Pan, zoom, and keep going.

bands.heading: Try it here
bands.body: Press N for a sticky, L for a connector, P for a pen. Nothing is saved.

bands.heading: The shortcuts you already know
bands.body: V, N, T, S, L, P, F. Marquee select, snap to neighbours, alt-drag to duplicate, space to pan. A tool people have to learn twice is a tool they abandon once.

points.title: What you can put on it
points.body: Sticky notes, text, thirty-two shapes, connectors with labels, freehand pen and highlighter, images, PDFs page by page, tables with merged cells, code blocks, embeds and mind maps that lay themselves out.

points.title: Frames, layers and snapping
points.body: Frames that carry their contents, layers, locking, alignment and distribution, snapping with spacing guides, and a minimap for the far corners.

points.title: Comments and presenting
points.body: Comment pins with threads, and a presentation mode that walks the frames in order. Live cursors and follow mode are built and have not yet been through a two-person session.

bands.heading: It works with the network unplugged
bands.body: The document is a CRDT in your browser. The server is where it goes to meet other people, not where it lives.

pages.title: Pages and databases | Tuval
pages.description: Pages with real blocks and databases with twenty column types, formulas, rollups and relations. Table, board, calendar, gallery, timeline and list views over the same rows.
pages.claim: Write it down. Then ask it questions.
pages.lede: A page is a page until you give it columns. Then it is a database, and the same rows can be a table, a board, a calendar, a gallery or a timeline without being copied.

bands.heading: Twenty kinds of column
bands.body: Sort it, group it, filter it. This is the real table.

bands.heading: A formula is a column that works out its own answer
bands.body: Add days to a date, roll a related table up into a sum, count what is still open. Created, edited, who by, and the row number are all columns you never have to fill in.

points.title: Every block Notion has
points.body: Headings, lists, toggles, callouts, quotes, code with highlighting, tables, columns, equations in LaTeX, mermaid diagrams, bookmarks, embeds and a table of contents that reads itself from the headings.

points.title: Mentions and backlinks
points.body: Mention a page and it links; the page you mentioned shows who pointed at it. Mention a person and they hear about it.

points.title: Markdown, HTML, PDF, backup
points.body: Markdown, HTML, a real text PDF, and a backup of the whole workspace in one file that can be put back.

bands.heading: Collections are questions, not folders
bands.body: Everything of mine that is late. Everything tagged decision. Nothing is filed into a collection and nothing falls out of one when it changes.

pages.title: Issues, cycles and projects — a tracker in your workspace | Tuval
pages.description: Issues with keys, two-week cycles, projects, estimates, labels, sub-issues and blocking relations. In the same workspace as the board the idea came from.
pages.claim: The work, where the thinking already is.
pages.lede: A tracker in a different tab is a tracker somebody forgets to open. This one holds the same records the canvas and the pages hold.

bands.heading: Group it however the question is shaped
bands.body: By status, by person, by priority, by cycle, by project.

bands.heading: A cycle is two weeks of work
bands.body: The next one starts where the last one ended. What did not finish moves, the burn-down says whether it was ever going to, and nobody runs a meeting to find out.

bands.heading: The parts that usually go missing

points.title: Keys that mean something
points.body: TUV-14 is the fourteenth issue in this workspace, taken on insert, never reused, and safe to write in a commit message.

points.title: Relations that read both ways
points.body: This blocks that, so that is blocked by this. Stored once, so the two can never disagree about which way round it is.

points.title: Time logging
points.body: Log a stint against an issue and the week adds itself up. Repeating work is asked for every night, so a missed night catches up.

bands.heading: It came from somewhere
bands.body: Select a sticky on a board, turn it into an issue, and the card stays exactly where the thought was. Open the issue and the board is one click away.

pages.title: For software teams — planning, retros and architecture | Tuval
pages.description: Sprint planning, retrospectives, architecture drawings and the issue tracker in one workspace. The sticky from the retro becomes the ticket in the cycle.
pages.claim: The retro sticky is the sprint ticket
pages.lede: Most teams run the workshop in one tool and the work in another, then spend an hour moving the first into the second. Skip that hour.

bands.heading: Start where you already start
bands.body: Kanban, retrospective, brainwriting, flowchart, mind map, architecture, five whys.

bands.heading: Monday morning, in order
bands.body: Open last cycle on a board. Drag what did not finish into the next one. Turn the three new stickies into issues without leaving the canvas. Close the tab.

points.title: Planning
points.body: Cycles of two weeks, estimates in points, a burn-down that counts the same set the list shows.

points.title: Design
points.body: Architecture on the canvas, mermaid in the doc, and one button that hands the whole flow to an agent as a brief.

points.title: Retros and decisions
points.body: A retro board, decisions written down as pages, and an incident record that links to the decision it changed.

bands.heading: The API is a door, not a demo
bands.body: API keys, webhooks and an MCP server, so n8n, a script or a coding agent can read and write the workspace. We integrate rather than clone.

pages.title: For client work — workshops, findings and handover | Tuval
pages.description: Run the workshop on a shared canvas, keep the findings as records, and hand over a workspace the client can still read next year. Read-only links need no account.
pages.claim: The client sees the room, not the cabinet
pages.lede: A workshop is worth what survives it, and a deck is not what survives it. The board they watched being drawn is the workspace the work is tracked in.

bands.heading: The room, on a screen everyone can see
bands.body: Comment pins, presentation mode through the frames, and a link that needs no account.

bands.heading: A link, not an invitation to install something
bands.body: Open a board to anybody with the link and it opens read-only, with no account. Or invite by email, or let a whole email domain in at once.

bands.heading: From the room to the handover

points.title: Decisions with their reasons
points.body: What was chosen, what it was chosen instead of, and why. Linked to the incident that prompted it.

points.title: Projects that hold their work
points.body: A project holds its boards, its pages and its issues, and the switch at the top of the sidebar makes everything else disappear until you switch back.

points.title: Everything, in one file
points.body: A backup of every page, board, issue, database, tag and link, which can be restored into their own workspace, self-hosted, with no licence to buy.

bands.heading: Read-only means read-only
bands.body: Viewer access is decided by the database, not hidden in the interface: a viewer who opens the console is refused by the same policy the screen obeys. Every one of those policies is checked by a suite that runs against the real schema before a change ships.

pages.title: Self-hosting — run the whole workspace yourself | Tuval
pages.description: AGPL-3.0. Run Tuval on your own machine with your own Postgres and storage. Every limit is yours to set, and the data never leaves.
pages.claim: Run it yourself. Nothing held back
pages.lede: The hosted plan is a convenience, not a lock. The same code that runs the hosted one is the code you can run, and there is no edition with the good parts missing.

bands.heading: Five commands
bands.body: The source repository publishes shortly. Once it does, point Tuval at your Supabase project, apply the migrations, lift the hosted-service limits, and build the folder of static files.
lines: cp .env.example .env.local   # add your Supabase URL and anon key
npx supabase db push   # apply the schema
psql -c "update public.tuval_settings set self_hosted = true where id = 1"   # lift seat, storage and API limits
npm install && npm run build   # serve dist/ from anything

points.title: A Supabase project
points.body: Hosted Supabase or the self-hosted stack. The schema is a folder of migrations you can read before you run them.

points.title: Object storage
points.body: The private Supabase Storage bucket created by the migrations holds images and attachments behind signed URLs.

points.title: Any static file host
points.body: The app builds to a folder of files. Anything that can serve them with the documented SPA fallback will do.

bands.heading: Nothing is held back
bands.body: No separate edition and no feature flags. Seats, storage and the API are limited on the hosted plan because those are what cost money to serve; on an install you run yourself they are not limited at all.

bands.heading: Access is decided by the database
bands.body: Every rule about who may read or write what is a row-level security policy, proven by a suite of access checks that runs against the real schema before any change ships. An interface that hides a button is not security; this is.

bands.heading: And you can leave
bands.body: One file holds every page, board, issue, database, tag and link, and restores into any workspace.

pages.title: Pricing — free for small teams, paid to be hosted | Tuval
pages.description: Free for up to three people with every feature. The paid plan is for people who would rather not run the servers. The code is AGPL and self-hosting is unlimited.
pages.claim: The code is free. The disks are not.
pages.lede: What is priced is somebody else running it: the disks, the bandwidth and the answering. Billed in lira, since that is the currency a Turkish company can take.

points.title: Up to three people
points.body: Everybody in the workspace, not per board.

points.title: A gigabyte of files
points.body: Images, PDFs and attachments across the workspace.

points.title: Every board, page and issue
points.body: Databases, publishing and forms included. The API and webhooks are the one thing held for the paid plan, and they are open on an install you run yourself.

bands.heading: Team
bands.body: Up to two hundred people, ten gigabytes of files each, and the API, webhooks and MCP server so n8n or a coding agent can reach the workspace. Everything on the free plan as well. Run it yourself and the seat count stops applying.

bands.heading: Working alone does not mean needing less
bands.body: It means the tax of moving between four tools is paid by exactly one person. Three people and a gigabyte is a whole workspace, not a trial, and no feature is held back to make the paid plan look thin.

bands.heading: How you pay
bands.body: There is no card form yet. The first thirty customers are invoiced and pay by bank transfer: write to product@tuval.dev with your company details, an invoice comes back the same week, and the workspace is on the Team plan the day it is paid. A card checkout arrives when it is worth the fee; being invoiced is not a worse deal, and for a Turkish company it is usually the one accounting prefers.

bands.heading: Or none of the above
bands.body: Run it on your own machine and every limit here is yours to set. That is not a downgrade path; it is the same code.

pages.title: A self-hostable alternative to Miro | Tuval
pages.description: An infinite canvas you can self-host under AGPL-3.0, with pages and an issue tracker beside it. An honest comparison with Miro, including where we lose.
pages.lede: A canvas with frames, connectors and thirty-two shape kinds, plus the tracker and the pages the board feeds into. Run it on your own Postgres.

rows.tuval: AGPL-3.0 licensed. The source repository publishes shortly; there is no separate edition and no feature flags.
rows.them: Proprietary, delivered as a hosted service.

rows.tuval: Your own Postgres and any S3-compatible bucket. One setting marks the install self-hosted and the seat, storage and API limits stop applying.
rows.them: Not offered.

rows.tuval: Free for up to 3 people with 1 GB of files. Hosted plan {price} per {per} per {period}, VAT included, about {about}.
rows.them: Per-user subscription. We do not print a figure we cannot keep current; see their pricing page.

rows.tuval: Sticky notes, text, thirty-two shape kinds, connectors with more than one label, pen and highlighter, images, PDF import up to thirty pages, tables with merged cells, code blocks, embeds, mind maps, comment pins, presentation mode, minimap.
rows.them: A comparable set of objects, plus diagramming and presentation features Tuval has not built.

rows.tuval: Eight board templates and four database kits.
rows.them: A large first-party gallery plus a public community library. Far more than eight.

rows.tuval: Yjs CRDT over Supabase Realtime, on private channels checked by the same row-level policies as the board. Live cursors and follow mode are written and have never been run through a two-person session.
rows.them: Multiplayer editing in production use for years.

rows.tuval: None. Desktop browser only, by decision rather than backlog.
rows.them: Native iOS and Android apps.

rows.tuval: Snapshots inside the board document, automatic every ten minutes, last twenty kept.
rows.them: Version history on paid plans, with longer retention.

rows.tuval: Imports a Miro board through their REST API with a token you supply that stays in your shell. Also images, PDFs and a Markdown brief.
rows.them: Not applicable.

rows.tuval: PNG of any selection, one JSON backup of the whole workspace that restores, and a one-click brief that turns the board into markdown with a mermaid flow for an AI agent.
rows.them: Image and PDF export and a documented REST API.

rows.tuval: REST API, webhooks and an MCP server for coding agents. No app directory and no built-in Slack, Jira or Figma connectors.
rows.them: A large app marketplace and first-party integrations with the tools most teams already run.

rows.tuval: Enforced in Postgres row-level security: editor and viewer roles, access by email domain, public read-only links, per-page roles. No SAML SSO and no SCIM.
rows.them: Enterprise identity controls including SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning.

bands.heading: Why you might not
bands.body: Because a decade-old product will not fall over in front of your client, and ours has never been through a two-person session.

bands.heading: What we do better
bands.body: Three things. The canvas is not a separate product: select a sticky, turn it into an issue, and the card stays exactly where the thought was while the issue appears in the cycle. The board exports as a brief an agent can act on rather than a picture, and an MCP server lets Claude Code or Cursor read the workspace directly. And you can run the whole thing yourself under AGPL-3.0, on your own Postgres and your own bucket, with nothing held back.

bands.heading: What Miro does better
bands.body: Almost everything to do with maturity. Their multiplayer has been carrying workshops for years; ours is written and unproven with two people in the room. They have native mobile and tablet apps; we have decided not to build a phone layout at all. They have thousands of templates and an app marketplace; we have eight templates and a REST API. They have a support organisation, published security certifications and enterprise identity provisioning; we have an issue tracker and one maintainer.

bands.heading: Who should not switch
bands.body: Anyone whose whiteboard is client-facing and unrehearsed. Anyone whose team joins from phones or tablets. Anyone who needs SAML SSO, SCIM or a signed support agreement to get software approved. Anyone whose workflow depends on the template gallery or on connectors to Jira, Slack or Figma. And anyone who cannot spare a person to run a Postgres database and a bucket.

pages.title: A self-hostable alternative to Notion | Tuval
pages.description: Pages and databases with twenty column types, six views, formulas, rollups and relations, self-hostable under AGPL-3.0. An honest comparison with Notion.
pages.lede: Pages on a block editor, databases with twenty column types and six views over the same rows, and an infinite canvas those records can sit on.

rows.tuval: AGPL-3.0. Run it on your own Postgres and bucket; a setting marks the install self-hosted and the limits stop applying.
rows.them: Proprietary, hosted only.

rows.tuval: Free for up to 3 people with 1 GB of files. Hosted plan {price} per {per} per {period}, VAT included, about {about}.
rows.them: Per-user subscription. We do not print a figure we cannot keep current; see their pricing page.

rows.tuval: Twenty. Thirteen you fill in and seven worked out, including formula, rollup, created by and edited by.
rows.them: A comparable set, including several Tuval has no equivalent for.

rows.tuval: Six: table, board, gallery, calendar, timeline, list. Filters, one sort at a time, grouping, per-column footers.
rows.them: A comparable set and more view types than Tuval offers.

rows.tuval: Headings, toggle headings, lists, callouts, quotes, highlighted code, tables, multi-column layouts, LaTeX equations, mermaid diagrams, bookmarks, embeds, table of contents.
rows.them: A wider block set. Synced blocks and links to a specific block are things Tuval has not built.

rows.tuval: Reads the export as it arrives: the zip of Markdown pages and CSV databases, including the multi-part zips a large export comes as. Folder nesting becomes page nesting.
rows.them: Not applicable.

rows.tuval: Per page: Markdown, HTML and a real text PDF. Whole workspace: one JSON file that restores into another install. Uploaded files are not in it, and the screen says so.
rows.them: Markdown, HTML, PDF and CSV export.

rows.feature: Two people in the same page
rows.tuval: No. A page is a CRDT that saves every two seconds and merges on open, so two people converge rather than overwrite, but you do not see each other type.
rows.them: Live co-editing with presence.

rows.tuval: Threads live inside the page document, so they cannot drift from the text they mark. The cost: the server cannot read them, so there is no workspace-wide list of comments waiting on you.
rows.them: Comments the workspace can query, with an inbox.

rows.tuval: Loads up to five hundred records per kind and filters them in the browser. Right for hundreds of rows.
rows.them: Databases far larger than that, queried server-side.

rows.tuval: The same records open as an issue with a key, cycle and estimate, or as a card on an infinite canvas. Forms drop answers into a database, and pages can be published.
rows.them: Pages, databases and forms, with no infinite canvas of its own.

rows.tuval: Neither. No phone layout, by decision, and no AI assistant in the product.
rows.them: Native iOS and Android apps and built-in AI features.

bands.heading: Why you might not
bands.body: Because your workspace is bigger than a few hundred rows, or your team writes in the same page at the same second; we merge, we do not co-edit.

bands.heading: What we do better
bands.body: A page here is a record, and so is an issue, and so is a card on a canvas: one row seen from three screens. A decision written up in a page can be the same object as the ticket that implements it, and a database of projects can be dropped onto a whiteboard as cards without being copied. The export is real: one JSON file holds every page, board, issue, database, tag and link and restores into an install you run yourself, under a licence that cannot be withdrawn.

bands.heading: What Notion does better
bands.body: Live co-editing, which we do not have. Scale, which we do not pretend to have: five hundred records per kind, filtered in your browser, is a small-team ceiling. A comment system the server can see, so there is an inbox of what is waiting on you. A richer block set, synced blocks and links to individual blocks. Mobile apps. AI. And an ecosystem that took years and a company to build.

bands.heading: Who should not switch
bands.body: Anyone with a wiki of thousands of pages or a database of tens of thousands of rows: the in-browser filtering will not hold, and we would rather say so now. Anyone whose team drafts documents together in real time. Anyone who reads and edits on a phone. Anyone who has built a workflow on AI writing, synced blocks or an integration directory.

pages.title: A self-hostable alternative to Linear | Tuval
pages.description: Issues with keys, cycles and estimates, in the same workspace as your boards and pages. AGPL-3.0 and self-hostable. An honest comparison with Linear.
pages.lede: Issues with workspace keys, two-week cycles, projects, estimates, labels, sub-issues and blocking links, on the same records as the board the idea came from.

rows.tuval: AGPL-3.0. Run it on your own Postgres and bucket; a setting marks the install self-hosted and the limits stop applying.
rows.them: Proprietary, hosted only.

rows.tuval: Free for up to 3 people with 1 GB of files. Hosted plan {price} per {per} per {period}, VAT included, about {about}.
rows.them: Per-user subscription. We do not print a figure we cannot keep current; see their pricing page.

rows.tuval: A workspace key taken on insert and never reused, four priorities, a numeric estimate, labels, an assignee, a due date, sub-issues by parent, and blocking and relates-to links stored once so the two sides cannot disagree.
rows.them: The same fields and more, including custom fields Tuval does not have.

rows.tuval: A fixed set of seven. You cannot add, rename or reorder them.
rows.them: Workflow states you define, per team.

rows.tuval: Fixed fourteen-day cycles one after the other, with a burn-down of points closed against points taken on. The length is a constant in the source.
rows.them: Configurable cycle length and a fuller planning model around it.

rows.tuval: One workspace, one issue prefix. There are projects, but no teams with their own prefixes, workflows or cycles.
rows.them: Teams, each with its own key prefix, workflow and cycles.

rows.tuval: j and k to move, c to create, x to select, Enter to open, a command palette, and g-then-key to jump between screens. Nothing fires while you are typing.
rows.them: A deeper and more complete keyboard model, which is what the product is known for.

rows.tuval: An issue is the same row as the page and the canvas card. Turn a sticky from the retro into a ticket in place; drop existing issues onto a board as cards that refresh their title and status.
rows.them: Issues, projects and documents, with no infinite canvas.

rows.tuval: Log a stint in minutes against any record and the week adds itself up. Rules create recurring issues daily, weekly or monthly, keyed on the date so asking twice makes nothing twice.
rows.them: Not part of the core product; teams add it with third-party tools.

rows.tuval: There is none. The CSV importer lands rows in a database, not in the tracker, so an export does not become Tuval issues. This is the hardest thing about switching.
rows.them: Importers from the common trackers.

rows.tuval: REST API with keys hashed at rest, webhooks, and an MCP server so a coding agent can read and write the workspace. No GitHub, GitLab, Slack or Figma integration; branch and pull-request linking does not exist.
rows.them: Git provider, chat and design-tool integrations, including the pull-request linking most teams build their habits on.

rows.tuval: No phone or tablet layout, by decision. Desktop browser only.
rows.them: Native iOS and Android apps.

bands.heading: Why you might not
bands.body: Because there is no importer, the seven workflow states are fixed and nothing talks to GitHub; switching costs you your history and your automation.

bands.heading: What we do better
bands.body: The tracker is not in a different tab from the thinking. A sticky on the retro board becomes an issue where it stands, keeping its place in the frame and its connectors, and the issue links back to the board it came from. The same record opens as a page or as a row in a database with formulas and rollups over it. Time logging and recurring work are built in rather than bolted on.

bands.heading: What Linear does better
bands.body: Nearly everything a tracker is judged on. Custom workflow states, teams with their own keys and cycles, configurable cycle lengths, saved views and insights: we have a fixed seven states, one prefix and a fourteen-day constant. Their keyboard model is deeper than ours and it is what the product is famous for. They have importers, so moving in takes an afternoon; we have none. They link branches and pull requests; we do not talk to GitHub at all.

bands.heading: Who should not switch
bands.body: Any team with issue history worth keeping: there is no importer, and asking people to retype a backlog is how a migration fails. Any team whose process needs its own states, its own team prefixes, or a cycle that is not two weeks. Anyone whose review flow runs through branch and pull-request linking. Anyone who triages from a phone.
